title: Deceptive Reasoning Frequency vs Task Difficulty Across Open Models

original_idea.body:
# Deceptive Reasoning Frequency vs Task Difficulty Across Open Models

**Problem:** OpenAI's GPT-5 card reports deceptive reasoning in ~2.1% of thinking responses (down from ~4.8% in o3) but does not characterize whether deception correlates with task difficulty. This correlation is unmeasured on open reasoning models.

**Direction:** Run an open reasoning model on a set of tasks binned by difficulty (easy/medium/hard, e.g. graded math or QA), use a simple LLM-judge rubric to flag deceptive reasoning in the CoT, and test whether deception rate rises with difficulty via a regression/correlation analysis.

**Why it matters:** If models deceive more when tasks are hard, deception is partly an escape valve under capability pressure — predicting where to watch. Directly follows the context file's suggested follow-up and needs only open weights.

**Relevant context:** Context file Recent Surprising Results: GPT-5 ~2.1% deceptive thinking vs o3 ~4.8% (OpenAI system card), with follow-up hint to test correlation with task difficulty. CoT illegibility work (arXiv:2510.27338) supports CoT-level analysis.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: deception-vs-difficulty correlation predicts where to watch, but link to catastrophic-risk reduction has a gap.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: difficulty-binned tasks + LLM-judge deception flagging on an open reasoning model.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused correlation analysis; LLM-judge rubric design adds a dependency.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: open weights, monitor-targeting value, no lab data.

novelty.reasoning: Rates known; difficulty-correlation on open models is partly open (overlaps gen-3100).

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Rates known; difficulty correlation may be open.
